lessons.title: Rock and Pop: The Features That Give the Style Away

practice_questions.text: Describe the standard band line-up you might expect to hear in a rock or pop track.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correctly named instrument or voice, up to 3 marks (e.g. lead vocals, electric guitar, bass guitar, drum kit, keyboards/synths).

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a backbeat.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the accent on beats 2 and 4; 1 mark for naming the snare drum (or equivalent) as the usual instrument.

practice_questions.text: Give the difference between a straight feel and a shuffle (swung) feel.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing straight feel as even subdivision of the beat; 1 mark for describing shuffle/swing as uneven, long-short subdivision.

practice_questions.text: Name and describe the role of a riff in a rock or pop song.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a riff as a short repeated pattern; 1 mark for naming a typical instrument (guitar or bass); 1 mark for describing its role, e.g. holding a section together or acting as a hook.

practice_questions.text: Outline the verse-chorus structure of a typical pop song, including the role of the middle eight.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for: intro sets up the song; verse carries changing lyrics; chorus repeats the same words/melody as the high point; middle eight is a contrasting passage after the second chorus. Up to 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of production that are typical of modern pop music.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for each correctly described feature, up to 4 marks. Accept: use of loops (short repeated sections); layering of multiple parts; synthesised/electronic sounds; four-on-the-floor dance beat. Award 1 mark for naming the feature and 1 mark for a brief description.

lessons.title: Music for Stage, Screen and Games

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a leitmotif, giving an example of how a composer might use one.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a leitmotif as a short recurring musical idea; 1 mark for linking it to a character, place or idea; 1 mark for a valid example of use (e.g. the motif returns whenever the character appears, telling the audience they are present or nearby).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between diegetic and non-diegetic sound in a film, using an example of each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for diegetic sound being sound the characters can hear within the story; 1 mark for a valid diegetic example (e.g. a radio, a band playing on screen); 1 mark for non-diegetic sound being sound only the audience hears; 1 mark for a valid non-diegetic example (e.g. the film score, a narrator's voice-over).

practice_questions.text: Name and describe the purpose of an 'I want' song in a musical.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as an early song in the show; 1 mark for describing that the main character states what they want or their goal; 1 mark for explaining that this drives or sets up the plot that follows.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by mickey-mousing in film music, and describe one effect it can have on an audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for describing mickey-mousing as music that closely matches the timing of on-screen action; 1 mark for a valid example (e.g. a rising scale under a character climbing, a falling slide under a comic pratfall); 1 mark for describing an effect (e.g. adds comedy, or makes an action feel more dramatic or emphasised).

practice_questions.text: Describe how an ostinato can be used to build tension in a film score.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an ostinato as a short pattern repeated continuously; 1 mark for describing that further layers or instruments are added on top over time; 1 mark for linking this build-up to an increase in tension or drama for the listener.

practice_questions.text: Game music must loop indefinitely and react to the player. Explain why this creates a different compositional problem to writing music for film or theatre, and describe one technique composers use to solve it.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a game's duration and path are not fixed, unlike a film or show with a set running time; 1 mark for explaining that the music must therefore repeat seamlessly without becoming tiresome; 1 mark for describing a technique such as vertical layering (layers added or removed to react to gameplay) or horizontal re-sequencing (jumping between pre-composed sections); 1 mark for linking the technique to reacting to what the player is doing in real time.

lessons.title: Study Piece: Queen — Bohemian Rhapsody, Seven Seas of Rhye, Love of My Life

practice_questions.text: Name the texture of the opening vocal section of Bohemian Rhapsody.
practice_questions.marks: A cappella homophonic/chordal (homorhythmic also creditworthy).

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of Seven Seas of Rhye.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Ten-bar instrumental introduction opening with a two-bar arpeggiated piano riff in octaves.
• Ten-bar verses; an eleven-bar first bridge and an eight-bar second bridge; a guitar-led instrumental solo.
• No chorus — the melodic hook 'the seven seas of Rhye' does the chorus's job; outro quotes 'Oh! I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside' and fades.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways recording technology shapes the sound of Bohemian Rhapsody.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of:
• Around 180 vocal overdubs building the choral textures.
• Multitracked/overdubbed electric guitars.
• Panning of voices and guitars across the stereo field.
• Flanged cymbals ('any way the wind blows'); reverb on the piano.

practice_questions.text: Explain how tonality is used across Bohemian Rhapsody.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Opens in B flat major (a cappella and ballad sections), moving towards E flat major.
• Abrupt modulation to the unrelated key of A major for the opera section.
• Hard rock section in E flat major; the song ends in F major — a different key from where it began.

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of metre in Bohemian Rhapsody and Love of My Life.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both are fundamentally in 4/4 (simple time).
• Bohemian Rhapsody interrupts it with single bars of 5/4 and 9/8, and its rock section switches to 12/8 compound time.
• Love of My Life stays 4/4 but slips in a single 3/4 bar in each verse, a 6/4 bar before the instrumental bridge and a 2/4 bar before the solo.
• In both, the changes serve the vocal phrasing rather than a dance feel.

practice_questions.text: 'The three Queen study pieces show three different ways to build a song.' Describe the main structural differences between the three tracks.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Bohemian Rhapsody: through-composed chain of six contrasting sections (a cappella, ballad, solo, opera, rock, outro) with no chorus, unified by returning material and key relationships.
• Seven Seas of Rhye: compact hard rock design — riff-based introduction, verses and two bridges of irregular lengths (10/11/8 bars), instrumental solo, no chorus, quoted-song fade-out.
• Love of My Life: ballad form — piano introduction, verses with instrumental bridge and guitar solo, coda; sectional repetition with varied scoring (harp, guitar).
• Credit precise supporting detail: keys per section, bar counts, the hook standing in for a chorus.

lessons.title: Placing a Track in Time: Rock, Pop, Broadway and Screen by Era

before.content_html:
Why the date matters

Section A plays you music you have never heard. The question is not only “what can you hear?” but “where does this belong?” Your exam covers four areas of popular music, and each is tied to a period: Broadway from the 1950s to the 1990s, rock of the 1960s and 1970s, film and computer gaming music from the 1990s onwards, and pop from the 1990s onwards.

You are not asked to guess the year. You are asked to hear the features that belong to a period and name them. This lesson gives you those features.

Rock of the 1960s and 1970s

The clearest clue is that the band sounds like people playing together in a room, because that is usually how it was recorded. The tempo breathes slightly instead of staying machine-exact. Drums are acoustic and you can hear the room around them.

Listen for electric guitar with overdrive or fuzz, the Hammond organ or electric piano, and a bass guitar playing a real line rather than a synthesised one. Vocals are often double-tracked, but never pitch-corrected.

Structures are verse and chorus with room for an instrumental solo. Later in the 1970s some rock grows more ambitious: longer forms, changes of metre and whole album sides given to one piece.

Key Fact — The Timing Test

Ask yourself whether the drums are perfectly even. Human drumming pushes and pulls very slightly. A grid-exact beat almost always means programming or a drum machine. Those have been common since the early 1980s, so an exact beat rules out the live-band rock of the 1960s and 1970s.

Pop from the 1990s to now

Modern pop is built rather than performed. Drums are programmed or sampled and quantised, so the beat does not drift. Underneath sit synthesiser pads and bass, and often a loop that runs through the whole track.

Vocals are the giveaway. They are layered, close-recorded and heavily treated, and from the late 1990s onwards you may hear pitch correction. Everything is compressed so the whole track sits loud and level.

Structure is tighter than in older rock: a short introduction, verse, a pre-chorus, then the chorus, often with a stripped-back middle section before the last one.

Broadway from the 1950s to the 1990s

Broadway spans fifty years, so listen for where in that span an extract sits. The 1950s bring a large pit orchestra with lush strings and a singing style closer to the classical tradition. Songs carry the plot: an opening number that sets the scene, and a song where the main character states what they want.

From the 1960s and 1970s, rock and pop instruments arrive in the pit — drum kit, electric guitar, electric bass. By the 1980s and 1990s you meet the big sung-through musical: little or no spoken dialogue, amplified voices, synthesisers alongside the orchestra, and themes that return across the whole show.

Film and gaming music from the 1990s

Orchestral scoring never went away, and a full orchestra with leitmotifs remains common. What marks out the modern period is the blend: orchestra layered with synthesisers, electronic percussion and sound design, and driving ostinato patterns under action scenes.

Game music has one feature film music does not need. It cannot know how long a scene will last, so it is written to loop seamlessly, and it often changes in layers — instruments are added or removed as the action intensifies rather than the music simply stopping and starting.

Putting it together in the exam

Name the feature, then let it place the extract. “The drums are programmed and exactly on the grid, and the vocal is layered and pitch-corrected, so this is pop from the 1990s or later” earns marks twice over: it describes the music and it supplies the context.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of these rules out a live rock band of the 1960s or 1970s?
options: Drums quantised exactly to the beat

knowledge_checks.q: What does double-tracking a vocal mean?
options: Singing two different melodies at once
Recording the same vocal twice and layering it
Splitting the vocal between two speakers

knowledge_checks.q: Which feature is typical of the big sung-through musicals of the 1980s and 1990s?
options: Amplified voices and synthesisers alongside the orchestra

knowledge_checks.q: Why is game music written to loop?
options: The composer cannot know how long a scene will last
A short theme attached to a character, place or idea
A key change at the end of a song
The loudest moment of a score

flashcard_questions.a: A live band sound with slight tempo variation, acoustic drums with room sound, and overdriven electric guitar with organ or electric piano.
flashcard_questions.q: Name three features that suggest rock of the 1960s or 1970s.

flashcard_questions.a: Programmed drums quantised to the grid, synthesiser pads and bass over a loop, and layered vocals that are heavily processed and sometimes pitch-corrected.
flashcard_questions.q: Name three features that suggest pop from the 1990s onwards.

flashcard_questions.a: From a large pit orchestra with lush strings and classical-style singing, through rock and pop instruments arriving in the 1960s and 1970s, to sung-through amplified megamusicals with synthesisers by the 1980s and 1990s.
flashcard_questions.q: How does Broadway change between the 1950s and the 1990s?

flashcard_questions.a: Game music must loop seamlessly because the length of a scene is unknown, and it usually layers instruments in and out as the action intensifies.
flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes game music from film music?

flashcard_questions.a: Listen to the drum timing. Human playing pushes and pulls slightly; grid-exact timing means programming or a drum machine, common since the early 1980s, so it rules out 1960s and 1970s rock.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the quickest test for whether a track was programmed or played?

practice_questions.text: Describe two features that would help you identify an unfamiliar extract as rock from the 1960s or 1970s.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for each feature correctly described, up to 4 marks. Accept: a live band sound with slight tempo variation; acoustic drums with audible room sound; overdriven or fuzz electric guitar; Hammond organ or electric piano; double-tracked but uncorrected vocals; an instrumental solo section.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the treatment of vocals differs between 1960s rock and pop from the 1990s onwards.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for each period. 1960s rock: recorded live or double-tracked, natural tuning, less processing. 1990s pop onwards: layered, close-recorded, heavily compressed and often pitch-corrected.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a Broadway extract from the 1950s might differ in sound from one written in the 1990s.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for each period. 1950s: large pit orchestra, lush strings, classically influenced singing, spoken dialogue between songs. 1990s: sung-through with little dialogue, amplified voices, synthesisers alongside the orchestra, themes returning across the show.

practice_questions.text: Explain why game music is written in loops and layers, and how this affects what a listener hears.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for the reason: the composer cannot know how long a scene or level will last. 2 marks for the effect: the music repeats seamlessly, and instruments are added or removed as the action intensifies rather than stopping and restarting.

practice_questions.text: An extract uses an orchestra with electronic percussion and a repeating ostinato under the action. Suggest what kind of music this is and justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying film or game music from the 1990s onwards. Up to 2 marks for justification: the blend of orchestral and electronic sound, and the driving ostinato typical of modern action scoring.

practice_questions.text: Using musical features rather than guesswork, explain how you would place an unfamiliar popular music extract in its period.
practice_questions.marks: Level 3 (5-6): several named features linked accurately to periods, with reasoning. Level 2 (3-4): some correct features named with partial linking. Level 1 (1-2): general comments about style with little musical evidence.
